en: Preface to the *Manlu* (Random Records) of Master Kuyā:
Shìxī and Yǎnxī loved people and esteemed the teachings of the sages; they were more eminent than the various elders of the Duan and Jiā eras.
In their later years, Lìngjìng was especially intimate with me, discussing and evaluating our writings without withholding a single word. He once said of Kuyā and Zhòngjiǎn: [text continues]
The two elders both subsequently served as record-keepers at Mount Jing. Jian was rich in literary talent, yet it is a pity he passed away young;

meanwhile, Kuya’s asceticism and indignation gave rise to a reputation for upholding the True Lineage. While I was staying at Heishiyan, a single *yuzhanhua* (jasmine) flower bloomed by the side of the path, and the autumn wind blew with a whistling sound.
Someone laughed and said, "As soon as a Chan practitioner sees this flower, they worry about warding off the cold, having no plan for what to do next."
He galloped westward and traveled far. He sat alone on withered cliffs and by broken windows, contented.

He would often take his bedding to the mountain crags to sleep together [with others], climbing towers when the moon was cool and gazing at the mountains after the snow had cleared; thus they shared a mutual sense of earnest sincerity within their hearts. I left Jǐnxī Bào cí and returned to Yánpíng Hánqīng for several years.
As we gradually drifted apart, I heard that Kūyá had compiled a collection of ancient texts into a record, and Yǎn xī rejoiced in this.
These recorded encounters all contain points for people to enter. Later, Chuncun remarked, "When shall we discuss the importance of brewing tea?
Zhuxi remarked, "In the future, we shall together be included in the *Sengbaozhuan*. When Guyan returned south, he brought these records to visit me;

it happened that I had just moved to Guangxiao Temple, so I glanced over them briefly before parting. Now, Guyan is flourishing in the world at Xingfu Temple in Quannan, and has begun compiling the *Qichang*.
The Master commissioned this to be carved in woodblocks and intended to write a preface. Indeed, Chanfang Zhengyan possessed a stern and incisive intellect;
his refined style and lofty character inspired the greedy and strengthened the weak—this is fully evident here.

Consequently, he thought of carving the old writings of Shixi Xianju Taibai, Zhongxuan Fufei, Feian Guang, Genyan Yi, and Shengsou Ding, as well as those of Huang Zhushan, in response to [the request].

It should be neither rhymed nor overly terse; Kuya shall excavate its remnants and compile them in succession, so that after the Five Lamps, another lamp may once again shine its light upon the world.
How could this be a mere random compilation? Kuya, whose name is Wu, is a native of Fucheng in Fuzhou.
On the second month of spring in the eighth year of the Xianchun era, Beishan (Shaolong) wrote this at Gushan.
The Old Chan Hermitage.
Formerly, when Chan Master Fuzhi of Yanxi resided at Lingyin, I was a guest in Lin’an. We visited one another regularly;

our spiritual connection and mutual accord were not of a single day’s duration. I had long known the fame of Kuya, yet we had never before met face-to-face. It happened that I was staying there by chance...
At the spring, he passed by Xingfu Temple. Upon seeing him once, it was clear that he was originally a man of the inner chambers;
he was serene, simple, and spoke little—truly one who had come from the lineage of Yanxi.

Recently, I heard that in the Guihai year (1233), Guyan returned to Mengtang at Mount Jing, where he compiled the karmic conditions for entering the Way as heard and witnessed from various patriarchs throughout his life, along with his public discourses and fragments of inscriptions, recording their names.
That which has not yet been inscribed upon the lamp—following whatever was committed to brush—is called the *Manlu* (Random Records). Its intent lies therein;

it was presented to Yǎnxī, who rebuked me and struck it down, saying there was no business for it within the closed door. In the fifth month of summer that year, he suddenly said to me: "I had thought that what you have written..."
This collection of miscellaneous records on efficacious anecdotes was intended merely as material for conversation. Upon reviewing it now, I find it is otherwise.
Among the recorded sayings, those that possess a point of entry to guide people have been marked with my pen; the rest have been struck out. Furthermore, I entrust you to preserve this with care.

Although I had wished to see this record, I had not yet had the leisure to inquire about it. Suddenly, Dajian Yuan rose from his seat and brought his original draft to me, intending to have it carved into printing blocks.
He requested that Xian’an provide a turning word (a *luanyu*). I examined and responded to him several times;

although these were things I had heard and seen during my time at Kuya, I compiled them into a biography—whether as praises, as *nian* (seizing upon a moment), as recorded words (*zhuoyu*), or as factual accounts. One...
Flowing forth from one’s own breast—how could this be merely relying on the original gourd?
Thus we know that what the Venerable Kuya compiled were all the beautiful jade within the casket, and not the "rat-jade" (a worthless stone).
What Chan Master Fozhi selected were all the stray pearls from the running platter, and not the eyes of fish. Were I to add further words, I fear it would instead produce flaws in the jade.
Yet it has become a flaw in the pearl. Because of my elder brother’s earnest entreaty, I could not refuse; thus I once again lowered one foot to assist him in painting the snake. Alas!
The publication of this *Manlu* (Random Records)—how is it different from Yang Xiong’s *Cao Xuan*, which incurred the ridicule of others? Nevertheless...
"In future generations, there will surely appear those who compose works such as the *Zixu*.
Summer of the Ren-shen year of the Xianchun era. Preface by Chen Shuzhen of Xina in Qingzhang.
*The Random Records of Master Kuya*, Volume One.
When Chan Master Zongzhao Yuan of Yuntong first arrived in Quannan, he was hosted by Wooden Hermit (Mukan). One day, having prepared the proper ceremonial demeanor, Zongzhao asked, "I am dull-witted;
I beg the Master to point out a place of seeing for me. Wooden Hermit pointed to the incense burner before him and said, "Do you see it?
Zongzhao replied, "I see it. Wooden Hermit asked, "How is it that you see it? Zongzhao said, "I do not understand. Wooden Hermit said: [The text ends here.]

Furthermore, it is said that upon seeing [the Buddha], he was struck with awe and attained awakening; sweat poured down his back. From then on, he shut himself within his door, never venturing forth for four years.
Wearing a single robe of a hundred patches, his refined bearing was lofty and ancient, such that no one could distinguish him as either intimate or distant.
Chan Master Cihui of the Zu-pai lineage was a native of the Zhang clan from Wenzhou. He received the tonsure at Luohan Temple in Kaiyuan.
He studied under Zongji, a successor of Wen Guansi. A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the True Dharma Eye?"
He replied, "Universally. Again, a monk asked, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? He replied, "Blind. The monk asked, "How do you understand this? Pai was at a loss.
Because of this, he became so anxious that he forgot to eat or sleep. One night, sitting until the hour of Zi (midnight), he heard a mountain bird call out once and attained awakening.
At dawn, he went to seek Zong’s certification. As soon as he entered the gate, he called out, "Master! Zong said:

The Master said, "Son, what have you come for? Baipai replied, "The handle of the ladle in the eastern house is long; the handle of the ladle in the western house is short. Guishan Zong asked, "Have you gone mad during the night?
Baipai said, "Is it the Master who is mad, or is it I who am mad? Guishan stepped down from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "What principle have you seen?
Baipai replied, "I humbly wish the Master good health and all blessings. Guishan let go of him and said:
"Return to me the *huatou* from the day before yesterday; I shall designate it as a woman’s prostration. He then presented a verse, saying:
"When asked about the True Dharma Eye, the answer was: 'Universally blind. Ten thousand li of clear wind, a single stream of bright moon.
Today, the fragrant clay image remains at Sisaong in the village, held in veneration by both monastics and laypeople.

Huang Zhuangding Gongzu Shun was particularly detached in his later years. He devoted himself to the Chan school and attained enlightenment through the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
He composed a verse, saying: "Six years I have devoted myself to reading the Buddhist scriptures, Yet time and again the words on paper have blurred my vision.
This morning, having let go of it all, there is nothing more to do; I am simply that same old man from before. He served as a high-ranking official and was a renowned statesman of the Shaoxing era.
Furthermore, as for those who were able to penetrate and realize this Way, Zhu Xi, Xu Xun, Pei Xiu, and Li Ao have monopolized the glory of the past.

When Chan Master Fuxin of Zhe arrived at Shuangjing, he met Master Ren, a successor of Dahui, and questioned him regarding the essential points of resolution sought by the assembly of seventeen hundred monks at that time.
He received the "Mu" (No) kōan—“Does a dog have Buddha-nature?”—and departed with its meaning silently realized. Upon passing through...

Tai’s Bao’en Temple sought a definitive resolution from Fozhao during a night session. Upon hearing the Master cite the World-Honored One’s words regarding the "shadow of the whip"—"One who acts upon seeing the shadow of the whip is not a fine horse"—he attained awakening at that moment.
The following morning, he entered the room and asked: "When one does not think of good..."
Do not think of evil. At this very moment, what is the original face of Elder Yan? He replied, "Even the Buddha’s hand cannot block it.
Later, while attending the veteran monk Zheng in Fanyang, he heard a nearby monk discussing the story of Yunmen’s "falling into a trap," asking, "Where exactly did this monk fall into a trap?
At that moment, he suddenly and clearly perceived the workings of Foguo Chuanzhu’s former kōans.
Usage. Every time Fozhao spoke to others, he would say: "Since I have held the handle of the whisk, the only one who has truly accorded with my spiritual capacity is Yan alone.
Later, Fozhao and Foxin succeeded one another in occupying Lingxiao; both their Dharma assemblies were flourishing, as if the Buddha-sun were still present.
Foxin’s stupa is located east of the stream; it is detailed in the commemorative inscription.

The Master Ruirang Lianchan of Xinghua Commandery was a native of that province. He styled himself the "Elder Huanzhu. Of remarkable talent from his youth, he had thoroughly experienced the monastic communities (*conglin*).

Having long attended Deng’an, he later received the Dharma from Dong’an, through which he realized the essential point of the mind. After returning to his hometown, he lived at the Tiger Hill Cliff for over ten years.
There, he composed several short verses on mountain life; one of them says: "A guest comes to inquire about the secret; the secluded birds speak in song."
"Chuan! This meaning is perfectly clear; what need is there for me to speak further? During the Jiading era, the Prefectural Governor invited him to Dongta, but he did not go.

Later, when he moved his staff to Ruixiang, he received the news of Dong'an's passing. He performed the rites of mourning and offered incense, saying: "In the past, I traveled abroad following the path of faith;
driven by the winds of karma, I have arrived at the borders of Mingzhou. Having settled at the humble hermitage of the old, blunt-headed one, I have suddenly encountered [this loss]."
Poisonous hands bring mutual ruin and harm; a fierce tiger emerging from the forest is not enough to inspire awe, and a venomous snake blocking the road is not yet considered strange.
As the void presses in and sparks fly, a foul reputation spreads through the monastic groves. Having found life amidst death, one returns once more.
Coldly reflecting on this, it is truly unbearable. I have recently heard that the somersault has already been turned upside down.
How joyful that in this era of peace and prosperity, our Way is flourishing! I offer this incense to express my earnest devotion, thereby settling the debt for the fist and the bamboo staff.
Monks, since Master Fozhao was thus, tell me: right now, is this an act of redressing an injustice, or is it a repayment of kindness? Speak!

Although this record is not worth half a penny’s worth of paper, who would have known that there was a man of true understanding who cherished it? The place where Ruixiang attained realization is clear;

he steadfastly maintained his resolve and refused to conform to the world. As the *kāṣāya* fluttered amidst the shimmering water and the shadows of the forest, one could perceive his lofty spirit and elegant character, enough to dissolve the worldly mind of any observer.
When Chan Master Tiebian Shao went to attend the opening of the hall by Mian Shanwai, he strode straight forward and said, "This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
those whose minds are empty return with the highest degree. At this moment of meeting you today, wind and thunder arise across the great earth. What is the matter of this meeting?
Mian did not answer. Tiebian spoke again: "Within the twelve hours of the day, there is a man who comes brandishing a sword to cut you down."

[The Master] went out. [The monk] thought, "What can I do with him? He still did not answer. [The Master] then struck his sitting mat once and said, "When meeting such an enemy, when would I wait to strike you?
Still, he did not answer. [The Master] withdrew and gave three salutations, saying, "I have captured the head-thief Yuan Da and Li Mo;
I await your instructions. The Hermit then raised a fist and showed it to him, saying, "I have received your instructions. [The monk] performed a somersault.
Doudou then came out. After entering the abbot’s quarters and finishing his duties, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"Just now there was a fellow with teeth like a forest of swords and a mouth like a basin of blood, holding a trailing rope in his hand that looked like an iron whip. I, the old monk, personally received a blow from him."
"You all must take great care. From this point on, he shall be known as Tiebian (Iron Whip). For six years, he served as an attendant who did not attend to administrative affairs.
Master Wannan Rou addressed the assembly, saying: "The phrase with a line and the phrase without a line are like a vine leaning against a tree in a thicket of brambles."
Open up the living path. When the tree falls, the vines wither. Where do the words return? A cast-iron scale-weight is eaten by worms;

setting down the clay basin, one laughs heartily. The sword that kills and the blade that gives life—if you are a true offspring of the golden-maned lion, you will see the absurdity from three thousand miles away.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, it is said: taking seven steps around the world, he had already entered the path of error; looking back with his eyes—
In the four directions, he opens his eyes and wets his bed; pointing at heaven and pointing at earth, what a strange sight! “I alone am honored”—this is still merely the talk of a descendant.
After all, he was bathing someone else; what did he hope to achieve? After a long silence, he said: “A thousand rows of tears upon a coral pillow.”
"Half is thinking of you, half is resenting you. Reading these few words, one knows that by treading on frost one anticipates ice, and by walking in dew one anticipates heat.
Although Milmam’s school was strict and exclusive, he received people very extensively; how could a fish large enough to swallow a boat ever slip through his net?
Chan Master Jieta Cong entered the quarters of Master Muan. One day, while attending him, he suddenly encountered his master’s anger, who said:
"What are you doing here? The summer retreat is nearly over; how do you understand the meaning of the West? Just as he was about to answer, he was struck across the mouth with a slap.
With a stern voice, the master said: "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As soon as he was about to answer again, he was struck another slap.

Suddenly, he had a realization and broke into a sweat; he prostrated himself in gratitude and departed. From then on, among those in various regions who called themselves practitioners of the Way, there were none who did not go to visit him and seek his stimulation.

Later, he resided at Shengyin Monastery in Wumen, where his reputation spread even further. With white hair falling to his shoulders, the monastic community referred to him as "Cōng the White-Headed One."

Chan Master Zhenyuan Huiri, whose courtesy name was Mingke, was square-jawed, lofty, and outstanding. His verse on the Three Barriers of Huanglong says: "My hand is the Buddha’s hand; A dustpan and a broom.
Picking them up and walking away— Who can distinguish which comes first? My feet are a donkey’s feet; Step by step I tread upon them.
I tread through empty space; Let others speculate as they will. Every person has their own karmic affinity; When the roof leaks, one looks toward..."
He saw the blue sky. Last night, the clay ox leaped about; the Diamond of the Hermitage went mad. When Ying’an saw this, he sighed and said, "Truly a bone-and-son descendant of Huanglong.
He composed a verse on the bamboo rattle, which says: "For half a year, the army has marched out to the ancient frontier pass."
The General rides alone on his steed with a towering resolve; One knows not that he has already broken through the heavy city, Yet he still holds fast the secure gate and will not let anyone pass.
When Dahui heard this, he said: "This is a descendant of Huanglong who also understands the discourse under Yangqi.
Zhenyuan once asked a monk: "The Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of one great matter. What is this one great matter?"
Regarding the causal conditions of this matter, the assembly remained silent. He then further offered an analogy, saying:
"Suppose a single bright pearl were suddenly placed in the marketplace at the head of the Chao Tian Gate. Thousands and tens of thousands of people pass by without seeing it.
Suddenly, one man encounters it and cries out, 'I am happy! Is this principle understood? When he first resided at Hangzhou..."
He possessed great merit. Later, he resided at Xingjiao in Shengzhou and Xiangshan in Mingzhou. He was a monk of the Wan’ian lineage of Tiantai, a descendant of Xuechao.
His speech and his fundamental tenets were like wood and water, possessing a deep and original source. In a separate note by Xuechao, it says:

"I am glad that you have come as my special messenger to receive this letter, and that you have been appointed to Lin’an to be selected for the abbacy. Furthermore, I have learned that since we parted, things have changed anew."
I am deeply comforted that you, the Abbot, are in good health and peace. I intended to visit you while traveling to Changlu, hoping to meet you there;
however, I learned that you had already entered the monastery. People say that great fortune currently resides deep within the mountains of Qianxin in Quanzhou.
This has left me with nothing but regret. I have no one else by my side and look forward greatly to your return; alas, it seems you have already departed, leaving me empty-handed.
The seal of kingship: it is difficult for both matters to be fulfilled simultaneously. For now, exert yourself and press forward in the practice of the Way;
do not indulge yourself to the point of being self-indulgent, making yourself thick while making others thin. You are well aware of this state of being soft, warm, and insipid;
nowadays, many who reside in monasteries are like this, so you may believe me. If autumn arrives, I shall certainly return to the Wannian Monastery on Mount Tiantai.
At the Avalokiteśvara Hermitage, I must make plans for a permanent departure; there will be no further opportunity to see you.

For now, please take care of yourself and act in accordance with worldly propriety, so that the light of our ancestral teachings may shine forth. My sincerest wishes. Pudian records only the Dharma-successor, the Head Seat Fachang.
Chan Master Aitang Miaozhan resided at Shuinan Hermitage within Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, serving as the water steward and the sanitation steward.

One day, while holding a fan to solicit alms before the temple, he was suddenly struck by a profound realization; so startled was he that he forgot to withdraw his arm. A monk standing nearby rebuked him, saying:
"You simpleton! There is money on the fan. As he broke into a sweat all over his body, [Zhaozhou] escorted him back to Baishui Hermitage and granted him certification (inka).
He also presented a verse to him, which said: "A single Buddha atop a mound of excrement, Emitting rays of light that illuminate heaven and earth."
A lotus blooms within the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals; this is simply because while washing one’s face, one touches the nose.

On the day Aikō served as the head of the assembly, the new Governor of Fukushū, Wang Gongdu, visited the mountain and found his views to be in perfect accord with him. Upon arriving at Fukushū, he was invited by Huangbo.
Later, he went to Wumen at the request of Governor Zhao Gongyanxu of Shouchen. It was only then that he passed away peacefully. Aikō was a native of Anji.
Rough and rustic, utterly devoid of literary embellishment; his occasional utterances were like withered firewood. People did not have the opportunity to see him—what a pity!
Chan Master Fuxing Song of Shaolin on Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture was born into the Xu family of Pucheng, Jianzhou.

He received his training at Mengbi Peak under Dajue and served as a "Grateful Returner" (Baoben) in Anji during an auspicious era. He succeeded Dong’an, and his reputation for the Way spread in all four directions.
Before long, he was invited to reside at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou. Entering the hall, he raised an ancient case: A monk asked Yanguan, "What is the original body of Vairocana?
Yanguan said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher. When the monk brought the pure water pitcher forward, Yanguan said: [The text ends here.]
He returned them to their original places. He remarked, "Yanguan’s eighty-four thousand pores were all wide open;
his three hundred and sixty joints were about to break apart. It is a pity that this monk was like one in a dream. He ascended the hall and raised this [case].
Dongshan said, "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, brothers, go east or west; go directly to where there are ten thousand miles and not a single blade of grass.
Later, the Hermit of Liuyang said, "As soon as you step out the door, it is all grass. Dayang said, "Even if you do not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse.
[The Master] comments: "Like sounds responding to one another and like vapors seeking one another—there is no doubt that these three great elders were of one accord."
If you examine this closely, it is all nothing but rattan vines encircling one's feet. But where lies the point of danger?

Who knows that atop the thousand peaks beyond the clouds, there is another spirit-pine, cold with the rain? He ascended the hall and said: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are utterly extinguished.
There are thousands of clusters of spring blossoms, and thousands of folds of spring mountains. At such a time as this—"
“Śākyamuni has lost his nostrils. Do you all know it yet? He gave a shout and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
“If you wish for the Great Function to appear before you, you must immediately forget all views. When all views are exhausted, the thick mists will not arise;
great wisdom will be transparently clear, no longer being anything else. He then raised his whisk and said: “Look! Look! If you say...”
[The Master] said, "I see it. It is like placing a head upon a head. If you say you do not see it, I shall cut off your head to seek life for you.

After a long silence, he said, "I have almost provided a mistaken footnote. He let out a shout and descended from his seat. Having retired from the assembly, he went to the Yan-shan Jiedai Temple in Wukang.
Emperor Ning held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem; during the Jiading era, he received an imperial decree once again to oversee Nanshan, which was immediately followed by another summons.
He had an audience at the Yanhe Hall and was granted the title Chan Master Foxing and a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya*; his honor and glory reached their peak.
Chan Master Kengtang Chong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Yuhang. He was a successor of Yan Wanan;

his demeanor was solemn and disciplined, and he was held in high esteem by his contemporaries. His verse on "The Mind Itself is Buddha" says: "As beautiful as Xi Shi when she left the Golden Palace, as graceful as..."
Empress Yang descended from the jade tower; all day long she was intoxicated with you beneath the flowers. What more could one find anywhere that is not elegant? Caoshan, drinking wine, said:
"A Persian merchant from the sea enters the Great Tang; he first secretly buries his treasures, yet comes back to stretch out his hand and seek them from others.
How can he hope to deceive those who are experts in the trade? He cited the words of the late Master Wanan, who said:
Sitting upon the Buddha’s seat, he cuts off the Buddha’s feet; he does not respect Confucius of the Eastern House, yet goes to a foreign land to practice ritual and music.
[The Master] picks up the staff and says: "To enter the mud and enter the water—this is not without our former teacher. But what can be done? The cold cicada clings to the withered tree;

its weeping is exhausted, yet it turns its head back. He strikes the staff and says: "Truly, there is one who does not turn his head back, who is willing to sit within the crucible. Kengtang [Dongshan Liangjie] was inside the crucible.

I pay you three prostrations. In the past, Daomian Foxing said: "In commenting on ancient cases (songgu) or picking up ancient cases (niangu), one must find the proper balance between extravagance and frugality.
It is like a person who knows how to spend money; it need not be much. Those who read the words of Kentang well will understand this for themselves.

The Master of Duan-an at Baofeng had long served under Fozhao. Seeing that there was a point of awakening in his verse on the karmic cause and condition of the Woman Emerging from Samādhi, one day he went to Fozhao’s chamber.
He stood with his palms joined at the left side of the seat; after a short while, he stepped out.
Fozhao called him forward, saying, "What have you to explain? Duan then stood with his palms joined at the right side of the seat. Fozhao shouted.

Chuan stepped forward with a respectful gait and departed. Zhao nodded his approval. Chuan was humble and modest like a commoner; he lived in a small hermitage without any provisions for the night, yet the shoes outside his door were always full.
His fellow disciples, such as Quan Guyun and Yin Tieniu, sent letters inviting him to come out, but he did not leave.
Chan Master Yuelin Guàn of Wuhui in Āngjì Prefecture was pure and sincere by nature, free from any affectation. He was the son of the Huang family of Hòuguān in Fúzhōu.

Initially a cowherd boy, he attained awakening while driving his oxen with a whip. He abstained from meat and blood and entered the monastic life under the guidance of the practitioner Zhōng of Xuefeng.
He received full ordination at the hands of Jièzǔn of Èrshèng in Jīngnán. Later, he met the venerable elder Zhèng of Dǐzhōu and obtained his [Dharma] transmission.

When Fa was first building a hall, he heard a story being recounted which said: "If one can turn things over, that is the Tathāgata. [Fa asked: "How would you turn over this incense altar right before you?
[The master] replied: "It strikes and it bumps. [Fa] was then rebuked and sent away. He subsequently attended upon [the master] as an attendant while traveling to Jianfu Temple in Rao.
Observe Yunmen’s “slipping into speech. Ten years later, one day while walking around a lotus pond, he recited to himself:
"Where is it that this monk slipped into speech? Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. Tudu was at Jingshan and Dun’an was at Huazang;

both sent letters inviting him to share the seat [of the abbot]. Regarding Dongshan’s "Three Pounds of Flax," he offered this verse: "The blue spots upon the lips of the guest leopard... [The tongue...]
The head monk of the capital city [said]: "Frequently calling for 'Xiaoyu' is originally of no consequence; it is simply that the patron wishes to recognize the voice.
During the Jiatai era, Shengyin of Wumen appeared in the world. He succeeded to the abbacy of Chengtian Wanshou, where students gathered like spokes converging at a hub.

While residing at Wu-hui, on the day he manifested illness, he still entered the inner quarters for a second time and said, "When the osmanthus flowers bloom, I shall depart," and he had his [disciples]...
I had merely joined the summer retreat when the osmanthus flowers were in full bloom—on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the Dingchou year of the Jiading era.
Before the morning session, I entered the room; the drum was struck again for the general discourse (*pǔshuō*). Once the assembly had settled, I took up my staff and said:
"With a staff, give a staff; without a staff, seize a staff. None among you have understood this; come forward and speak! The assembly...

Without resistance, he cast down his staff, sat upright, wrote a verse, and passed away. He had lived seventy-five years and spent fifty-one summer retreats. After his cremation, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. Alas!
This world-renowned master dwelt amidst life and death like the drifting of clouds or the flight of birds;
from the beginning, there was no obstruction. In the summer of the year of the Rooster, he entered *nirvāṇa*, and the cassia trees blossomed profusely, just as he had foretold. This is it.
This is especially seen in the place where his transcendent, wondrous, and clearly verified signs appear. Is this not the power of one who single-mindedly bears the Great Dharma?

Zen Master Cao Yuan-sheng was at Guifeng in Xingzhou. Addressing the assembly, he said: "From morning until evening, the bells, fish-bells, drums, and wooden clappers have already awakened the supreme capacity for all of you.
If you can believe it, then the sands of Ganges of Buddhas are present within each of you."
Under the heels of every person, there is a *pò* leaping about. If you do not believe this, Guifeng Shide will eat his rice with his mouth and strike the meditation seat!
Descend from your seat. This is what the True Huanglong meant when he said that one who is like a wealthy man of many generations does not spend a single coin in vain.
When Chan Master Songyuan Yue first entered Min, he visited Qianduan Mukan. After a long time, he took his leave; Mukan then nominated him.

"Up until now, it has not been found. [He] shouts, "What connection is there? He says again, "Sitting coldly, guarding a withered post;

those who lack a way to turn themselves around mostly miss the timing and lose the opportunity. Once it pierces to the very marrow of one's bones, it is a state of intimate and unobstructed joy—a spring breeze of perfect harmony.
For us monks, our two eyes are like bells; we glare fiercely, playing with the divine mechanism."
Wind and clouds are naturally distinct. Let them do as they please—pouring wine and burning paper money, bowing their heads to celebrate the New Year.
The wind whistles; the leaves flutter. On the wall, the mulberry branches stir; the willow branches suffer most. Northern Chan sings the village music, cooking the oxen of the open field.
They bustle and scurry—what can one do about it? They provoke others to gather up their hides and horns. A knife hidden within a smile. *Du!* Peace and tranquility.
The world need not employ the sword or spear. To recite this is like drinking jade-like nectar; it naturally causes one to regard even thin gruel and water lilies as sufficient.
Alas! Ku Chan may truly be said to have received the transmission, for he has fully realized that the milk of the Dharma originates from a single source and possesses no differing flavors.
Pizhi Yanzhu was a native of Yuxi who lived during the Jian’an era. Initially, he made his living by weaving double-strand thread.
Suddenly, he attained awakening and entered Mount Yinglin, where he abstained from grain and dwelt beneath a great tree.

When his wife and children pursued him with urgency, he shaved his hair and fled to Pizhi Rock on Nangshan beyond Putou. Later, he also accepted offerings from the laity and became a monk. He was pure and...
In the interval between these years, Magistrate Lin Xi-yi of the district invited [the Master] to the two Chan monasteries of Gui-shan and Chen-shan; he accepted only after being pressed.

Not long thereafter, longing for his former retreat, he wrote to his fellow practitioners, saying: "Now, those who bear the title of 'Abbot' serve as models for the assembly and act on behalf of the Buddha to propagate the teachings.
Yet, if one lacks the reputation for virtue, conduct, and moral integrity, and is ignorant of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and law..."
"By using grass mats and hempen robes, eating wood and drinking from mountain streams, I already feel ashamed; to present myself before others—how could I truly bear it?
I shall shake out my robes and return home directly. Such was his firm resolve regarding his conduct, which also served as an aid to the community of monastics.
Master Donggu Guang was of refined and transcendent spirit and possessed keen discernment; his realization of the Dharma reached its ultimate depth.
He shared the joy of the Dharma with Master Shizhai Jiang, who recorded three verses from Xian’an and sent them as a poetic response, saying:
"Do not say that West Hermitage is small; it is utterly without boundary or surface. To him who has come in person, every single direction is perfectly clear. Do not say that West..."
The hermitage is still; the roar of the iron ox resounds. The pillar and the lantern nod their heads in mutual response.
Do not say that West Hermitage is destitute; it swallows space and spits out space again. Meeting the Old Man of Jingu, he beats the drum of spring in the month of December.
Having resided at Lingyin, he grew weary and passed away suddenly. Master Dongjian Tang Han offered this inscription for his memorial: "The Master of East Valley was lofty..."
However, Master He was the master of Cold Spring. Not many days had passed since he first appeared, yet he manifested illness so early; how could his passing have been so sudden?
Although I have only recently come to know him, I shall speak the truth upon opening my mouth. My inquiries were earnest and sincere; though our traces may have been distant, our hearts were close.

Suddenly, he sent me a handwritten letter, an ancient painting, and famous calligraphy, arriving to announce his departure. Upon reading them, I was naturally overcome with grief. Examining the brushwork closely, it is truly vigorous and elegant. This is...
The person who has transcended all measure is one with the cycle of birth and death; yet my own ordinary sentiments move me to shed tears of sorrow.

Snow fills the lakes and mountains, and my feeble horse is difficult to urge forward. I merely hold this fragrant incense to pay my respects at his chamber. At that time, those who came and went to discourse on the Way were all renowned dukes and ministers;
this is what is called "people gathering at the gate."
When Master Jili Dan first resided at Puzhi in Huzhou, the place was desolate and secluded like a way-station.
For nine years, he sat in meditation day and night facing the sacred monk (the image). Later, he lived at Qionglong in Suzhou, where his teaching style became even more lofty and rigorous;
few were able to enter his room. He would often say within the hall, "Qionglong has a phrase. Whether a monk offers a response or fails to offer one, they are treated as one and the same."
Regarding "Beating and Scolding": Wuzu was serving as the Librarian (Zangzhu) in the assembly hall when he slightly offended [Zhaozhou], who had him expelled.
He said, "Tell him to stay at Jingshan, and then come see this old monk. Later, when Wuzu resided at Jingshan, he happened to leave while begging in Wumen;
there, the thorns were still at Huqiu. When the two elders met, they clapped their hands and laughed heartily.
Chan Master Kai of Yanshi at Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang Prefecture was a native of Chengdu.

Having traveled extensively through lecture halls, he suddenly grew weary of them and desired to cross the mountain passes to settle the great matter. The Grand Councilor, Duke An, also encouraged him with a verse, saying:
"I have a great affliction because I have a body; this body is a provisional combination and not real. Vimalakīrti manifested illness, yet it was fundamentally no illness. You should go forth..."
He traveled further south to Room (Shi) at Donghu Lake in Fanyang, where he encountered Songyuan.
Upon hearing the question, "Why does an enlightened monk lose his nostrils? he attained realization beneath those words.

One day, as Shi was reading a sutra, a fellow monk sitting at the same table asked him, "When you attain the seat and don the robes in the future, how will you teach others? Shi took the sutra and handed it to the monk.
The monk took the scripture and threw it onto the desk; Shishi picked it up again and recited it with a resonant voice. The monk then withdrew.
In the *Xinyou* year of the Jiatai era (1201), he first accepted an invitation to Yunju on Mount Lu. Before long, by imperial decree, he was appointed to Jinshan.

Like the Dharma talks of Lantian, his teachings were all direct shortcuts for Chan practice. Among all those he encountered throughout his life, he alone succeeded in inheriting the lineages of Fohai, Dachang, and Songyuan.
Master Shuangshan Yuan sat in his room and said, "In the abbot’s quarters of Baen, there is not one thing to be found.

I have won only the reputation of being someone who pushes others through the door into the mortar. He addressed the assembly, saying, "The monk of the patched robe does not know the size of the months, nor the intercalary days of the year."
While eating triangular *zongzi* rice dumplings, he remarked, "This is the Dragon Boat Festival. Suddenly, Bao'en moved him up to the first seat.
He ignored this, remaining half-suspicious and half-believing. This morning, as usual, [Bao'en] poured a cup of tea for him to moisten his mouth.
Abruptly, he bit into a *changpu* root; cold sweat broke out across his body, and he let out a cry of "Ahh! "That Fujian man is enough to drive one to distraction," he said. Great!
"Assembly! Is this not the medicine that penetrates the spirit? Thirty years hence, you must take care not to discard it.
As he entered through the three gates, he said, "There is an entrance at the head of the bustling marketplace; it is simply because you all have become calloused to seeing it.
The new Elder, as he walked, did not hesitate to swing his arms about. Looking back at the assembly, he said, "Follow me! Duality-Redwood remained firmly established.
At present, whatever comes to hand is nothing other than a marvelous elixir from the ancient masters—a method for transforming one's bones and a formula for raising the dead.
Why seek it elsewhere?
When Chan Master Jing-sou Jue was residing at Xia Lingyan, Chidu instructed him to contemplate the koan: "The dog has no Buddha-nature."

Upon hearing these words, he attained realization beneath the master’s voice. Consequently, he shared his insights with Chan Master Qian Wuyin. Wuyin said, "This is indeed so, yet your life-root has not been severed.
You must go out and see other teachers before you will truly succeed. He then instructed him to visit Master Chun’an.

When the old monk arrived at Huazang, he remained there for half a year without gaining anything. One day, suddenly hearing the sound of the fire-board, his stagnation was instantly released. He reported this to [Master Chun’an].
Chuan’an. As soon as Chuan’an struck the drum and opened the room for instruction, the Old Man (Shou) hurried in.
Chuan’an asked, “What is the Buddha? The Old Man replied, “Wildflowers bloom along the road. Chuan’an asked, “What is the Dharma? The Old Man replied, “Many people are intoxicated by private wine.
Chuan’an asked, “What is the Sangha? The Old Man replied, “The mouth of the alms bowl points toward the sky. Chuan’an said, “Not yet. Get out! Later, the Old Man stayed in the room of Chidu.
In the midst [of the assembly], when asked, "What is the Buddha? he answered with a thunderous voice, "A rotten winter melon.
He then spoke this verse: "What is the Buddha? A rotten winter melon. Biting into it, the frost penetrates the teeth. Though its root and stem have no hollow pit, Once a year, it blooms but once.
When Jingzou was among the assembly, he attained the power of non-concealment; the strength of his two pine trees was even greater.
Chan Master Xinfeng Beishan Xin of Fuzhou was a native of that province. His character was upright and stern, and his spiritual faculties were swift and keen.
When those who had first begun their studies met him, they frequently failed in their responses. Later, while he was at Gushan, a monk came for an audience.
Gushan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The monk replied, "Xichan. Gushan asked, "What sayings or phrases did Xichan have? The monk said, "The talk has fallen away. Gushan said:
"Where did you learn such things? The monk replied, "It is not fitting that I have offended the Master today.

Yunshan took up his staff and struck him. The monk snatched the staff away, laughed heartily, and departed. Yunshan then invited him for tea, remarking, "I heard that Old Xuan, the head seat, has already left.
Initially, Beishan and Yueku had traveled to Zhejiang together and visited Dun'an at Huayan.

In the past, Yueku of Zang had already attained realization and verification; thus, the Master was able to seek his counsel and resolve his doubts there. Later, upon returning to his native village, he visited Minghuishi and shared the teaching seat at Gushan.
When Zhao Gong Yifu, the Governor of Zhangzhou, heard of his Way, he invited him to the Southern Monastery.

Gushan declined and excused himself, saying, "Your Excellency has heard of me in error. Only after the invitation had been extended three times did he finally go. Upon opening the hall for the assembly, he offered incense in honor of his former companion, Yueku.
At that time, public opinion held him in high esteem.

Chan Master Kuchan Jing was by nature simple and austere; he had no personal preferences or indulgences, devoting himself solely to guiding his disciples and tirelessly engaging them in the rigorous testing of Zen dialogue.
When someone asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Kuchan struck the meditation seat once.
Nowadays, when people speak and reveal their words, not even a thousandth or a hundredth part of them can reach the level of the predecessors.
Furthermore, where does the point of vital importance lie? Do you understand?
Chan Master Chuijue Chong once accepted an invitation to Xuefeng in Fuzhou. He shared a long-standing friendship with the Minister Chen Wei, who invited him to his private residence for a meal.
There, he requested a eulogy for a portrait of Xiang Yu. The Master took up his brush and wrote: "Uprooting mountains was not due to physical strength;
surpassing the world was not due to mere spirit. With eight thousand followers, they conspired together to achieve their aim. To all people, he was known as the Great One under Heaven."
A vessel cannot be secured through the struggle of force; it must first rely upon benevolence and righteousness.

Little did they know that Heaven lent its hand to execute the tyrannical Qin, and subsequently enabled those who were broad-minded, compassionate, and loving toward others to become emperors. Alas! This indeed provided great benefit to this world.
The Duke was greatly amazed by this. Chijue’s wisdom and eloquence were vast and expansive; this [response] was merely a small remnant of his talent.
Chan Master Pingshi Jieshi was a native of Qinxī. His character was lofty and simple. A monk asked, "What is it like when a precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard?
He replied, "Where the cuckoo cries, the flowers lie in profusion. The monk asked, "What is it like after it has emerged from the scabbard? He replied, "It..."

People always remember General Li. A monk asked, "How is it when [the sword] has emerged and when it has not yet emerged? He replied, "The sword has long since departed; you are merely carving marks upon the boat.
In the summer retreat *shanghan*, he said: "For ninety days one restrains the feet; this is like a net catching birds in their nests.

For three months one dwells in peace; this is like driving away foxes to guard a tomb. Facing the place where life and death do not reach, one beholds three heads and six arms, overturning the perfect circle."

At the Jue Monastery, it was as if mooring a boat by holding onto a pillar. Before Mount Huangyun, beneath the twin *tao* trees, for ninety days, the wind blew at its proper time and the rain fell at its proper time;
throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, there was neither decrease when less was needed nor increase when more was required.

For three hundred and sixty days of the year, he remained in *an-ga* (meditative stillness) every day and performed *sva-asti* (self-liberation) at every moment. Those who were round were naturally round; those who were square were naturally square.
The square is square; the long is naturally long, and the short is naturally short. One cannot avoid stirring up dust upon the pure ground. Ultimately, how is it?
When the Great Garuda spreads its wings, the celestial path is vast; when the giant turtle turns its body, the ocean waters narrow. His public teachings were of this nature.
In his later years, he resided at Cold Spring in Hangzhou and named his quarters "Outside the Green Mountains. During the Jingding era, the Chancellor Qiuhuo Jia...
The Duke especially revered the Buddha-dharma. He submitted a petition and obtained imperial permission for [Yuan] to reside at Jingci Monastery. Later, Huaihai also succeeded him in the abbacy;
both had risen from the Dongjian (East Valley) community.
Zen Master Shitada Kō said: "When the Venerable Kō resided at Lingyin, he was also in a state of helplessness.
Being squeezed from the east and the west, he was pressed right up against the corner of his meditation seat with no way to evade it.
Having no choice but to act as a patriarch, he had to break through his mask and come forth, saying: 'In this place there is no vermilion; red earth is considered superior.'"
Nevertheless, when we look at the present age, it gradually becomes nothing but bare earth; people increasingly eat mud and soil.
To speak of this truly makes one’s heart shudder with cold. Alas! How should those who are resolved upon the Way feel when they hear this?
In the Jiaxi era, Chan Master Shuangshan Yuan was the first seat (*dìyīzuò*) within the Stone Field Hall (*Shítíntáng*).

He wrote a letter to the Chancellor, stating that the new imperial decree regarding the purchase of clerical titles (*shīhào*), gold rings, and elephant-head staffs (*xiàngjiǎn*) was inconvenient. The letter read:
"The thirteenth day of the first month. The former abbot of Tiantong Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture and current first seat of the Front Hall at Jingde Lingyin Chan Temple."
The temple monk Zhongyuan respectfully bathes himself in incense and offers this letter to the Grand Chancellor, State Duke, and Chief Councillor.
I humbly consider that the teachings of Buddhism and Daoism are expedients for saving the world.

That they may coexist with Confucianism within the realm of Heaven and Earth is due to their ability to awaken the true nature and prevent one from falling into heterodox views; their merit is not easily measured. Our dynasty’s Emperor Taizong...
The Emperor once remarked, "The Way of the Śākya clan provides a supplement to our teachings.
Emperor Xiaozong also said, "It is appropriate to cultivate the mind through Buddhism, to govern the body through Laozi, and to govern the world through Confucianism.

Zhang Wending stated that the Way of the Confucians is thin and insipid, and that the sages and worthies of their time all turned toward the Śākya clan; furthermore, the masters of the Guan and Luo schools also necessarily relished and savored the teachings of the Śākya.
Only after studying the works of these masters can one succeed in continuing the secret teachings that were not transmitted from the banks of the Zhū and Sì rivers.

Yet, every teaching must have a central authority and a teacher. Since the state permits individuals to purchase ordination certificates (*duò*), all who become monks must seek out a teacher to follow as their refuge.
If a teacher possesses the Way and its practice, they can cause the deluded to awaken and the obstructed to attain penetration; thus, they provide great assistance to the world.
The teachings must not be merely a minor supplement. In recent times, bribery has been practiced openly; those who seek to become abbots are the sinners of our religion.
If the succession were handed down according to such precedents, the worthy ones of the world would surely hide themselves deeply and flee far away.
How could they be willing to come forth and serve as teachers? If teachers are neglected, the True Dharma will decline; if the True Dharma declines, false teachings will flourish. [With] purity...
To treat these as gateways for the mutual pursuit of profit and desire is not a blessing for the state. It is like a family academy or a local school that cannot do without a teacher;
yet, if one does not seek someone capable of transmitting the Way and resolving doubts, but instead looks only to those who value bribes, how can the disciples look up to them?
The teaching of the School of Confucius would almost surely perish, and the same would be true for the Way of the Buddha and Laozi.

How is this different? If you say that the followers of Buddhism and Daoism dwell in grand mansions, daily enjoy rich delicacies, wear clothes without raising silkworms, and eat food without plowing the fields—thus being resented by the world—then there are even more people throughout the empire who live uselessly for the world yet sit and enjoy the same provision of rich delicacies;
why single out monks and Daoists? Furthermore, when temples and monasteries are first established, their permanent endowments...
This was provided as an offering, not because the government granted it to them. It was given because the common people delight in making donations.
Monasteries and observatories possess fields, and their tax burdens are especially heavy; furthermore, they have various non-essential requirements that are exactly like those of great households.
Now, since they purchase ordination certificates with money and pay for exemption from corvée labor with money, the government provides not even a thread or a grain of support, yet they merely—
If the pursuit of profit is allowed to continue without limit, then the clergy and the monastic order may be said to be truly unfortunate.
If the state lavishly bestows titles and honors indiscriminately, how can it encourage and inspire the world?

If monks and nuns obtain golden rings and ivory tablets through bribery and thereby secure positions as abbots in various temples, then those who are ignorant, wayward, and unprincipled will all advance by means of corruption; how then can one hope to rectify social customs?
Furthermore, although temples and monasteries are numerous, those whose permanent endowments are deficient are very many.
Even if this edict were implemented once, it could only compel the larger temples and monasteries to contribute; how could the smaller ones possibly meet such demands?
Under these circumstances, what could possibly be obtained? Moreover, monks and Daoists cannot simply provide their own wealth to serve as abbots; they must necessarily...
They are seized from temples and monasteries; masters and disciples slaughter one another, and the spirit of the permanent endowment (*sāṃghika*) is destroyed.

What was once fertile soil will soon be seen as overgrown weeds; what was once a great mansion will soon be seen as a mound of ruins; what was once warmth and satiety will soon be seen as cold and hunger.

Although there are official decrees for the various districts, who will petition for them? Although there are able-bodied men for each year, who will pay the taxes? Today, these are merely the military requisitions and the capital for grain purchases.
Examining all such certificates, none but those for the sale of noble rank; those who sell rank may bring ruin to the state, yet those with many such documents cause no trouble to the officials.
Thus, by following a temporary practice that shows no concern for the long-term, we have carved away the source of prosperity for thousands of millions of years.

This is hardly a sound long-term strategy for managing state finances. I have observed that the recent imperial decree to increase the price of money and sell titles has been criticized by those with discernment;
fortunately, the matter was not carried out. The current petition submitted by the General Administration is precisely of this same nature.

I humbly entreat Your Majesty’s compassionate wisdom to carefully weigh the benefits and harms and to specifically memorialize the Throne so that the order regarding the wearing of clerical robes may be entirely rescinded, thereby ensuring that monks and Daoists do not [violate their precepts].

I am most grateful for your favor. I humbly entreat your compassionate majesty to deign to consider this. With these incomplete words, I remain. At that time, Chan Wuwen of Jiangxi also sent a letter.
Previously, the imperial court, due to a petition by the Commissioner-General Yue Ke, had requested the bestowal of two ranks of purple robes and monastic titles.
He was granted a golden ring, an ivory tablet, and a four-character Dharma name for Chan Master.

When he resided at Ta’i Temple, every time he was granted robes, a title, or an embroidered paper (liñ-zhǐ), they were sold for three hundred strings of cash; furthermore, these were appended to the regulations for officials of rank.

No one without an official post could be appointed, and no one without granted robes could serve as abbot. When this petition was submitted, the matter was indeed quashed. Was this not divine protection?

How can one say that those who uphold the Great Dharma lack sincere devotion? Shanzhu of Shuangshan was able to reach the utmost in austere simplicity, devoting himself single-mindedly to the practice of the Way.
Like Jijian Tang, even when dwelling in private within a dark room, he acted as if facing a great guest and seemed as though he were a realized elder monk.
This is another instance of a wise man’s self-discipline, evident even in his most minute details. How truly virtuous he was!

Chan Master Kuzhuang Tan was pure and upright, speaking but little. He would sit in meditation emaciated throughout the entire day. He propagated the Dharma at Dayu Temple in Yue, which is also located east of the valley stream.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the Master has not yet seen the Buddha-mind? He replied, "When a person is poor, they turn to the Way. The monk asked, "What is it like after one has seen it?
He replied, "When one's dye is exhausted, it returns to black. He often presented ready-made koans and was able to speak upon them.
"Thirty blows! You cannot speak—thirty blows! A serving monk said, "I hope the Master will show compassion and grant me a skillful means.
He replied, "I took you for a fine steed out of the stable. The monk attained realization. (Kuzhuang; from Langzhou.)
Later, he resided at Tiger Hill (Húqiū) in Gūsū. Monastics and laypeople alike followed him with great devotion.

Master Yúnchāo Yán was tireless in his instruction and study; moreover, he was humble enough to lower himself before those of lesser status and treated them with profound kindness. Talented and eminent scholars sought refuge under him.
On the day of opening the meditation hall (kāilú), he addressed the assembly, saying: "This phrase is to be swept away; that phrase is also to be swept away. Xuefeng rolls [the ball]."
The ball. The carrying board of Muzhou. Only that old fellow Zhaozhou, at the head of the brazier, picked up the incense spoon and fire tongs;
he nudged them here and there until he suddenly struck upon a piece—a very old broken porcelain bowl from the corner of a wall in a household at Jingde Temple in Raoyang.
The Tathāgatas of the three periods simply watched. Yun’an said: "These words are remarkably similar [to those of Muzhou]."
His father was Songyuan Nanweng, the Chan Master Ming.
When he first entered the assembly, he was able to resolve his mind to practice Chan.

He once stayed overnight at the Stone Bridge on Mount Tiantai, where he encountered an extraordinary monk who directed him to see Old Focin. Upon reaching Mount Taibai, Nanweng surrendered himself with sincerity and entered that master’s Dharma.
As he was seated, he had barely opened his mouth when he was rebuked. He thought to himself, "If I do not attain realization in this life, there will be a future life.
Thereupon, tears flowed down to his chin. Later, while serving as an attendant in the assembly of Chidu, he stood in attendance during the evening sermon.
Hearing the bell toll, Chidu asked, "What sound is that? The Master replied, "The sound of the bell. Chidu said, "The sound comes to the ear; [where does the ear go?]"
Wangsheng went to see Wengboju, who had not yet replied when he was sharply rebuked by the Master. Sweat poured down his body;
only then did he say to himself, "It turns out that all the scoldings and insults Wuzhuo has directed at me over these years have been right to the very bone and marrow.
Previously, Wuzhuo had only instructed him to contemplate the story of Baizhang’s wild fox. One day, Dun asked, "What is it like when one neither falls nor is obscured? Wuzhuo responded immediately:
It is said: "Neither falling nor obscuring; a pair of mandarin ducks float and dive upon the water, moving with effortless ease.
Dunfu sealed this [verse]. The Master was a son of the Huang family of Quanzhou. He was a fellow traveler from the mountain passes with Nanshan Long.
After returning to his native village, he resided at Jiaozhong on the creek; he finally entered nirvana while staying at Nangshan in Puzhong.

Chan Master Xishan Liang was a native of Fuzhou. He was austere and lived with great frugality; he once possessed a single paper quilt that was nearly covered entirely with patches and repairs, yet he never changed it regardless of the cold or heat.
He served as the head of the abbot’s quarters at Gushan before responding to an invitation to Yunmen, and later moved to Huangbo.
He never once replaced his attendant monk. One night, [the monk] secretly exchanged the master’s silk quilt for another. Daoliang cried out in alarm and rebuked him, saying, "I have little merit;
throughout my life, I have never dared to wear silk. Moreover, this quilt has accompanied me for thirty years—how could it be discarded?
Those who heard this said that his conduct while dwelling in the mountains possessed the spirit of the ancients. Later, he retired from his position and entered Yongyang Yanmen.
In the mountains by the lake, he lived with practitioners who tilled the soil with knives and sowed by fire, remaining there until his end was unknown.
Chan Master Nantang Bian of Wanshou Monastery in Pingjiang Prefecture sent a verse to his fellow practitioners, which says: "The monkey and the turtle cannot be separated;
calling 'brother' and responding 'yes' seems like forgetting the self. Yet when the conversation reaches the point of paradox, it turns out to be the very heart and liver."
He brought nothing with him, yet he was renowned in his time. Later, as he sat upon the site of enlightenment, he advocated [the Dharma] as easily as rolling a ball down a slope.
Truly, he did not disgrace his father, Yan’ai, nor his grandfather, Yue’er Long.
Chan Master Biejie Peng said: "When Master Zhen of Biefeng retired from Gushan, he went to Yuwang to wait for an audience with Dahui.
He sat upon a single meditation cushion behind the Buddha Hall for seventy-nine days.

When the Lady of the State of Qin invited Dahui to ascend the seat [for a formal discourse], he rejoiced to himself, saying, 'Today I shall certainly see him. Indeed, he obtained an audience, and their conversation was in perfect accord."
Inside the hall, he further uttered three turning phrases and departed. Mahāmati was greatly amazed by this. Subsequently, he and Hongzhi together promoted [the teachings] and resided at Yuelin.
A pagoda still exists there in the temple today. Biefeng’s entire body was covered with long hairs, and he was commonly called "The Precious Lion.
Jishi inscribed his calligraphy, summarizing the account as such. Having already received the Dharma from Fo[yan], Biefeng...
Master Xincai sat loftily upon the eminent seat; his Way was already manifest. Yet he remained courageous in seeking an audience with Miaoxi. What was his intention?
His case cannot be compared to that of Poyi, who delayed his journey. This is precisely what constitutes the standard for a patriarch of an era. Alas!
Now, a mere junior student merely desires to wait ninety-seven days to behold the Venerable One.
It was also difficult for him to find lodging.

Chan Master Shoucheng was a native of Putian. Having completed his years of training and received full ordination, he dwelt in a cave beneath Mount Nang. He constructed a hut against the cliff, merely to shield himself from wind and rain.

His father served as a local official in the prefecture and provided him with a yearly ration of grain. Whenever guests arrived, he did not inquire whether they were seeking instruction in the Buddha-dharma.
The people of the world all stared at him with wide eyes. A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Hermitage Master? He replied suddenly, "Building a hut against a cliff;
scooping up stream water to cook porridge. The monk asked further, "If someone were to ask about the meaning of the Westward Journey, how would you respond?"

He wiped his tears with the back of his sleeve and wept, saying, "How bitter and grievous! Observing his refined disposition and exploring his profound intent, was he not a peer to those who have attained such resonance?
Master Chan Shiha Yue of Shixi said: "When I was thirty years old, I was about to travel south again. I heard the words of Master Kongsou."
I traveled as a wandering monk for twenty years; this matter was finally at rest. When I first received these words, my mind was deeply unsettled.
Later, passing by the desks of the two Sages and the Seat-Holders, I saw the words of Qionggu, which cited Yunmen’s "Falling into a Trap.

Within that luminous, silent illumination, there was suddenly a place of rest. Upon ascending Mount Ou, within ten days I joined the ranks and entered the room. My late teacher raised the case of Da...
